generic: Penicillin (natural penicillins: benzylpenicillin/Penicillin G and phenoxymethylpenicillin/Penicillin V)
quick: Pen G: 1-4 million units IV/IM q4-6h (severe infection); Pen V: 250-500 mg PO q6-8h
Pen V: take on an empty stomach (1 h before or 2 h after food) for best absorption
Considered safe; penicillins are among the preferred antibiotics in pregnancy
Compatible; small amounts in milk, generally well tolerated
Reduce dose / extend interval in significant renal impairment (renally cleared)
No routine adjustment for usual doses
Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis, renal function and electrolytes (Na/K with high-dose Pen G), signs of superinfection
summary: "Penicillin" is an ambiguous group term. This record is a class overview of the NATURAL penicillins - benzylpenicillin (Penicillin G, given IV/IM) and phenoxymethylpenicillin (Penicillin V, given orally). These are bactericidal beta-lactam antibiotics that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis and remain first-line for many gram-positive and selected gram-negative/anaerobic infections, including streptococcal pharyngitis, group A strep infections, syphilis (Pen G benzathine), and susceptible pneumococcal disease. Typical adult dosing is Penicillin G 1-4 million units IV/IM every 4-6 hours for severe infections and Penicillin V 250-500 mg orally every 6-8 hours. The dominant safety concern is hypersensitivity - immediate IgE-mediated reactions including anaphylaxis can be fatal; obtain a careful allergy history before use. Many staphylococci and other organisms are now resistant via beta-lactamase production.
indications: Streptococcal infections including pharyngitis/tonsillitis and skin/soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible group A streptococci
Prevention of rheumatic fever and recurrent streptococcal infection (Penicillin V or benzathine Penicillin G)
Susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae infections (e.g., pneumonia, otitis media) where susceptibility is confirmed
Syphilis and other treponemal/spirochetal infections (benzathine or aqueous Penicillin G, per stage)
Other susceptible infections: meningococcal disease, anthrax, actinomycosis, Clostridium and other anaerobic infections, diphtheria adjunct, erysipelas
Endocarditis prophylaxis/treatment for susceptible streptococci/enterococci (Penicillin G, often with an aminoglycoside)

dosage.d: 1-4 million units every 4-6 hours (up to 12-24 million units/day for serious infections such as meningitis or endocarditis)
dosage.n: High doses given by IV infusion; aqueous crystalline Pen G

dosage.d: 250-500 mg every 6-8 hours; pharyngitis often 500 mg twice daily or 250 mg four times daily for 10 days
Early syphilis: benzathine Pen G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose; neurosyphilis: aqueous Pen G 18-24 million units/day IV (3-4 million units q4h) for 10-14 days
dosage.n: Long-acting benzathine form for early disease

dosage.r: Penicillin V oral or benzathine IM
dosage.d: Pen V 250 mg twice daily; or benzathine Pen G 1.2 million units IM every 3-4 weeks
Reduce dose or extend the interval for Penicillin G in significant renal impairment (CrCl reduction); high-dose Pen G accumulates in renal failure
dosage.n: Watch for neurotoxicity/seizures and electrolyte load at high doses

admin: Obtain a careful penicillin/beta-lactam allergy history before the first dose; have resuscitation facilities available for parenteral use
Penicillin G is given by IV infusion or deep IM injection; aqueous crystalline form for IV, procaine/benzathine forms are IM ONLY (never IV)
Give Penicillin V orally on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) to maximize absorption
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve, to reduce resistance and relapse (e.g., 10 days for strep pharyngitis)
For high-dose IV Penicillin G, account for the sodium or potassium content in patients with cardiac/renal disease
moa: Penicillins are beta-lactam antibiotics that bind to and inhibit penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) involved in cross-linking the peptidoglycan layer of the bacterial cell wall. This blocks cell-wall synthesis and activates autolytic enzymes, producing a bactericidal effect against actively dividing organisms. Activity is time-dependent (efficacy relates to the time concentration exceeds the MIC). Resistance arises chiefly through bacterial beta-lactamase (penicillinase) enzymes that hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, and through altered penicillin-binding proteins.

absolute: History of serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema, severe skin reaction) to any penicillin or beta-lactam component
relative: Significant renal impairment (dose accumulation, neurotoxicity at high doses)
History of atopy/multiple drug allergies (higher reaction risk)
High-dose Penicillin G in heart failure/renal failure due to sodium or potassium load
monitor: Immediate and delayed hypersensitivity reactions (rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis)
Renal function and electrolytes (sodium/potassium) with high-dose Penicillin G
Signs of superinfection including Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea
CBC with prolonged high-dose therapy (rare neutropenia)

preg: Penicillins are considered safe in pregnancy and are among the preferred antibiotics; they cross the placenta but have a long record without evidence of teratogenicity. Benzathine Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for syphilis in pregnancy. Use when indicated.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding - only small amounts pass into milk and are generally well tolerated by the infant; rarely the infant may develop diarrhea, candidiasis, or a rash. Monitor the infant for these effects.
renal: Penicillins are eliminated mainly by the kidneys. Reduce the dose or lengthen the dosing interval in significant renal impairment, especially with high-dose Penicillin G, which can accumulate and cause neurotoxicity (myoclonus, seizures). Penicillin is removed by hemodialysis - supplemental dosing may be needed.
hepatic: No routine dose adjustment is required for usual doses in hepatic impairment. Rare cholestatic/hepatocellular reactions can occur; monitor if there is pre-existing severe liver disease.

major: Probenecid - blocks renal tubular secretion of penicillin, raising and prolonging penicillin levels (sometimes used intentionally)
Allopurinol - increased incidence of skin rash when combined with aminopenicillins (class consideration)
moderate: Methotrexate - penicillins can reduce renal clearance and increase methotrexate toxicity
Bacteriostatic antibiotics (e.g., tetracyclines, chloramphenicol) - may theoretically antagonize the bactericidal effect
Combined oral contraceptives - possible reduced efficacy (advise additional precautions, though evidence is limited)
minor: May reduce gut flora and slightly alter the absorption/effect of some drugs
interactions.food: Penicillin V absorption is reduced by food; take on an empty stomach. Penicillin G is parenteral and not affected by food.
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction with penicillins.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction (non-enzymatic) tests and may interfere with some urinary protein and direct Coombs tests; high doses may affect coagulation/aggregation assays.

serious: Anaphylaxis and other immediate IgE-mediated reactions (can be fatal)
Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS)
Neurotoxicity/seizures with very high doses or in renal failure
Hemolytic anemia, neutropenia, or coagulation abnormalities with prolonged high-dose therapy
rare: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction when treating spirochetal infection (e.g., syphilis)
Electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalemia/hypernatremia) from high-dose Penicillin G salts
emergency: Severe or bloody diarrhea (C. difficile colitis)

monitoring: Immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis - observe after the first parenteral dose
Renal function and serum electrolytes (sodium/potassium) with high-dose Penicillin G
Signs of superinfection and C. difficile-associated diarrhea
CBC with prolonged or high-dose therapy
Clinical response and culture/susceptibility results to confirm appropriate coverage
counsel: Tell your clinician about any prior reaction to penicillin or related antibiotics BEFORE taking this medicine
Stop the drug and seek emergency care immediately if you develop rash, swelling of the face/lips/throat, difficulty breathing, or faintness (signs of a serious allergic reaction)
Take Penicillin V on an empty stomach and finish the entire course even if you feel better
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea, which can occur even weeks after treatment
Women using oral contraceptives may wish to use an additional method during therapy
pk: Rapid bactericidal action; serum levels within minutes (IV) and ~30-60 min (oral Pen V)
Pen G IV: essentially immediate; Pen V oral peak ~30-60 minutes
Short-acting forms dosed every 4-8 h; benzathine/procaine Pen G provide prolonged release over days to weeks
Oral Pen V tablets at room temperature; reconstituted oral solution refrigerated and discarded after the labeled period; parenteral Pen G per product labeling
pearls: "Penicillin" is an AMBIGUOUS group term - this record covers the NATURAL penicillins (benzylpenicillin/Penicillin G IV-IM and phenoxymethylpenicillin/Penicillin V oral) as a class overview, NOT a single specific product
Hypersensitivity, including fatal anaphylaxis, is the key danger - always take an allergy history; have epinephrine/resuscitation ready for parenteral dosing
Penicillin G is parenteral (IV or IM); Penicillin V is the acid-stable oral form - benzathine/procaine Pen G are IM ONLY (never give IV)
Time-dependent killing: efficacy depends on time above MIC, favoring frequent dosing or continuous infusion for severe infection
Beta-lactamase-producing organisms (e.g., most Staphylococcus aureus) are resistant - natural penicillins are not appropriate empiric anti-staphylococcal therapy
Benzathine Penicillin G remains first-line for syphilis, including in pregnancy
missed: For scheduled oral Penicillin V, take the missed dose as soon as you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and do not double up. Try to keep doses evenly spaced and complete the full course. Missed scheduled parenteral doses should be addressed by the treating team.
overdose: Overdose with penicillins is uncommon but very high serum concentrations - especially with high-dose Penicillin G in renal impairment - can cause neuromuscular irritability, myoclonus, and seizures, and electrolyte disturbances from the sodium/potassium salts. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive (control seizures, correct electrolytes). Penicillin is removed by hemodialysis, which can be used in severe overdose with renal failure.
